The jury is still out on whether the other ingredients, such as taurine, gua-
rana, ginseng, and yerba mate, add a boost. A study of college football
players that compared a taurine-containing energy drink (AdvoCare Spark)
with and without caffeine suggested the caffeine is the primary “magic
ingredient” (Gwacham and Wagner 2012). Yet, too many emergency room
visits are related to overdoses of caffeine-laced energy drinks that result in
rapid heartbeat, muscle tremors, and seizures.

Like soft drinks, energy drinks are erosive, and can cause lasting damage
to teeth. Another concern about energy drinks is that many athletes and
sports fans use them as mixers with alcohol. The caffeine masks the effects
of the alcohol, so consumers may not realize how intoxicated they are. This
increases the likelihood of drunk driving (Ferreira et al. 2006; Marczinski
and Fillmore 2006).
